sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Bielefeld is the one city in our set where car parks have become steadily busier: occupancy was 6% above 2023 in 2024, 12% above in 2025, and is still rising (+2% on 2025 so far), while Germany has been flat. In the same garages, the average weekday went from 30% of spaces occupied in 2022 to 36% in 2025.

That is happening against the city's stated direction. Bielefeld aims to halve the car's share of trips from 50% to 25% by 2030 [0]. The Jahnplatz, the central junction, was rebuilt with EU money to a single car lane with more room for buses, bikes and pedestrians, and the Niederwall became a bicycle street [5][6]. A 2022 proposal to charge up to €4 an hour on the street was scaled back: in 2025 the coalition settled on €2 in the old town and city area (from €1.30) and €1 in the wider centre, to start once a new guidance system runs, expected from mid-2026, with resident permits left at €30 [2][3]. The local chamber of commerce rates the centre's attractiveness as falling, with parking among its weakest scores [13].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
Part of the rise in occupancy may come from supply leaving the market. The Kesselbrink parking structure was taken down from 2022 for a Goldbeck new build [7], Contipark's Ritterstraße garage was closed for four years of renovation before reopening in July 2026 with about 480 spaces and 30 charging points [8], and the former Karstadt complex is to be demolished for housing and shops [14]. With fewer spaces, the remaining garages fill up more, so rising occupancy here is not the same as rising demand.

Contipark is consolidating: besides reopening Ritterstraße it has taken over the 804-space Ankergärten garage [9]. The city counted 243 public charge points in 2024 and notes it can steer charging directly only in its own garages [11].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Bielefeld is compact and cheap. Almost every garage is within a kilometre of the Jahnplatz, and the typical price is €2 an hour and €12–14 a day, about two-thirds of Düsseldorf's. ORBE has the most sites and the lowest prices (€1.50, €10 a day). Contipark and Q-Park charge around €2.20, and the retailers' association ProEinzelhandel runs four central garages at €1.50.

Here, unlike most cities, price matters: dearer garages are emptier. APCOA is the most expensive operator, about 22% above its neighbours with a €23 day ticket, and its garages are nearly empty on weekdays (8%; the Neues Bahnhofsviertel garage 7%). The busiest garages are cheap and right in the centre: the Neues Rathaus underground garage (64%), Borchard's Am Zwinger at €2 (63%) and ProEinzelhandel's Am Theater at €1.50 (50%). The garages around the station have plenty of room, at about a quarter full (23%).
